old: I should have founded a city for him in Argos, and built him a house. I should have made him leave Ithaca with his goods, his son, and all his people, and should have sacked for them some one of the neighboring cities that are subject to me. We should then have seen
new: I would have founded a city for him in Argos, and built him a house. I would have made him leave Ithaca with his goods, his son, and all his people, and would have sacked for them some one of the neighboring cities that are subject to me. We would then have seen
reason: Butler's first-person 'should have' + participle is the Victorian conditional; Homer 4.174-176 is a past counterfactual ('I would have settled a city for him in Argos and built him a house'). In present-day English, American above all, 'I should have founded…' and 'I should have made him leave Ithaca' read as obligation or regret ('I ought to have'). That turns Menelaus's frustrated plan, which depends on the homecoming named in the sentence before, into self-reproach for a duty he neglected. The paragraph only corrects the reading at its last sentence. Only the auxiliary changes, in all four places, so Butler's one construction stays one construction. 'sacked' and every other word stand; see rejected_barriers for 'sacked'.

old: when they have taken in water
new: when they have taken in fresh water
reason: With ships as the subject, 'taken in water' is now the idiom for a vessel shipping water (leaking or swamped), so the harbor sentence says that ships put to sea after flooding. Homer (4.359, 'having drawn dark water') means drawing drinking water for the voyage. Butler's own phrase for this is 'Here we landed to take in fresh water' (9.4). Adding 'fresh' restores his phrase (D29), rules out the leak reading, and adds nothing the source does not mean.

old: for they had made sure that
new: for they had felt sure that
reason: This is a dead sense. Butler's 'made sure' means 'felt certain'; Homer 4.638-639 has 'for they did not think he had gone to Pylos'. A present-day reader takes 'make sure that' as 'ensure' or 'check', so the suitors seem to have verified or arranged that he had not gone. 'felt sure' keeps Butler's 'sure' (D29) and changes only the verb. The next sentence ('They thought he was only away…') partly corrects the misreading, so this is the milder of the two occurrences.

old: we had made sure that it would come to nothing
new: we had felt sure that it would come to nothing
reason: This is the same dead sense (Homer 4.664: 'we thought it would never be accomplished'). Here the context pushes a present-day reader toward the wrong sense and nothing corrects it. 'We had made sure [= ensured] that it would come to nothing, but the young fellow has got away in spite of us' reads as though the suitors had acted to stop the voyage, which they had not. It is the stronger of the two occurrences. The rendering is the same as B04-03.

old: A hind might as well lay
new: A doe might as well lay
reason: Outside hunting usage, 'hind' as the female deer is unknown to most present-day readers, and at the head of a sentence it reads as the adjective ('hind legs'). The simile turns on the animal: a grazing mother leaves her newborn in a lion's lair, and the lion kills them (Homer 4.335-339, elaphos, feminine). 'doe' is the current word for the same animal, keeps the female that 'her new born young' needs, and adds nothing. The continuity sheet (§5) keeps this simile 'limb for limb'; this repair changes the word, not the limb.

old: that we may rest in peace from now on
new: that we may live in peace from now on
reason: 'Rest in peace' is now fixed as the formula for the dead. A wish that 'we may rest in peace from now on' in the house just reached therefore sounds like a wish to die there. Butler, and Homer 4.34-35 ('if ever Zeus would give us rest from misery hereafter'), mean an end of wandering and hardship, and 'live in peace' is the current idiom for that. Everything else stands, including the prayer form 'heaven grant'. Butler's 'rest' is still current English, but the phrase no longer carries his meaning, which is the reason D29 asks for.

'Take nothing by' (= gain nothing from) is an obsolete idiom. The reader decoded it from context, but it is the one opaque phrase in the sentence that sums up what Odysseus got for his labors (Homer 4.107-108: 'for him there were to be only sorrows'). 'gained' is the plain verb for Butler's sense, and nothing is added or lost.

old: on the pretense of paying their addresses to my mother
new: on the pretense of courting my mother
reason: 'Pay one's addresses to' (= court) is a dead idiom, and a present-day reader is likely to hear 'paying their respects'. That loses the marriage suit, which is the pretext that explains why the men are in the house and the point Menelaus answers with 'usurp a brave man's bed' and 'a sorry wedding'. The reader recovered only by bringing in knowledge of the suitors from outside the sentence. Butler's own word for this is 'courting' (6.2, 'all the best young men among your own people are courting you'; 24.9, 'we were courting his wife'), so the repair uses his vocabulary (D29).

old: but presently I leave off again
new: but then I leave off again
reason: This is a dead sense in the present tense. Butler's 'presently' means 'after a little while' (Homer 4.102-103: 'at times I take my fill of weeping, at other times I stop again'). With a present-tense verb, a present-day reader takes 'presently' as 'currently', so Menelaus seems to say he has stopped grieving for now, not that each bout of weeping ends. 'then' carries the sequence, and 'again' still carries the recurrence. The Book's other two 'presently' (¶23, past narrative; ¶57, future) cannot be read as 'currently' and are kept.

old: the gods backed the wind into its old quarter
new: the gods turned the wind back into its old quarter
reason: 'Backed' is a sailor's term (a wind backs when it shifts against the sun), here used transitively. To a present-day reader, 'the gods backed the wind' says they supported it, and the reader could rebuild the sense only from 'and they reached home'. 'turned … back' is Homer's own verb (4.520: 'the gods turned the wind back'), and once the verb is clear Butler's 'its old quarter' can be read, so his noun is kept.

old: there was not one of you would so much as think of giving me a call out of my bed
new: there was not one of you who would so much as think of calling me out of my bed
reason: Penelope's rebuke has two stumbles in one clause. The omitted subject relative ('one of you [who] would') is no longer standard and trips the sentence, especially when heard (the edition has audio). 'giving me a call' is now the idiom for telephoning. Supplying the relative and turning Butler's noun 'call' into the verb keeps his word and his sense (Homer 4.729-730: 'to rouse me from my bed').

'Sea-horse' now names the small fish, which makes no long voyages. Penelope's image is that ships are men's horses on the sea (Homer 4.708-709, halos hippoi, 'horses of the salt sea'), and with the fish it becomes absurd or is lost. 'horses of the sea' opens Butler's compound into its own sense, which is also Homer's phrase, and adds nothing. Under PUNCTUATION §4 (D15) this changes what is said aloud, so it is a rendering decision to record in the continuity sheet, not a silent compound change.
